edits.before: ### 2. **Asarru al-nadamah**: Regret Becomes Too Deep Even for Speech
edits.after: ### 2. **Asarru al-nadamah**: They Hid the Regret — But From Whom?
edits.evidence: No fetched edition glosses asarru as speechlessness or depth of feeling. The question all four editions actually engage is the concealment's audience — al-Tabari and al-Jalalayn name it, al-Muyassar and Ibn Kathir leave it open. The retitle poses the question the sources answer instead of asserting an answer none of them gives.

edits.defect: The asserted psychological WHY of the concealment had no classical basis and was not marked as contemplation; the specific reason two of four sources DO give was omitted
edits.before:
That verb is striking. **Asarru**. They kept it hidden, held it inside, secreted it. The regret is real, immense, and undeniable, but it does not emerge as liberating confession. It sits inwardly as a sealed pain under the sight of punishment.

This is different from repentance.
edits.after:
That verb is striking. **Asarru**. They kept it hidden, held it inside, secreted it. But hidden from whom? The ayah does not say, and the commentators fill that gap in a way most translations leave out.

Al-Tabari reads it as the leaders hiding it from the led: the chiefs of these mushrikin concealed their regret from their lowly ones and their followers, once they saw Allah's punishment closing around them and were certain it was landing on them. Al-Jalalayn says the same and gives the motive — the leaders hid it from the weak ones they had misled, out of fear of being reproached — and reads the regret itself as regret over having abandoned faith. Al-Muyassar keeps it plain and unassigned: those who wronged hid their anguish when they saw Allah's punishment fall on all of them. Ibn Kathir's rendering stays general too — they would feel the regret in their hearts.

So in the reading al-Tabari and al-Jalalayn carry, the concealment is social before it is inward. Men who spent a lifetime being followed cannot let the followers watch them break. Even at the edge of punishment the image is still being managed, and the people it is being managed for are the very people they misled.

There is a second way to sit with the same verb, and it belongs to contemplation rather than to what the word itself states: regret sealed inside is regret that has lost its function. It never comes out as confession. It just sits there, real and immense and going nowhere.

Either way, this is different from repentance.
edits.evidence: al-Tabari 10:54: "وأخفتْ رؤساء هؤلاء المشركين من وضعائهم وسفلتهم الندامةَ حين أبصرُوا عذاب الله قد أحاط بهم، وأيقنوا أنه واقع بهم". al-Jalalayn 10:54: "﴿وأَسَرُّوا النَّدامَة﴾ عَلى تَرْك الإيمان ﴿لَمّا رَأَوْا العَذاب﴾ أخْفاها رُؤَساؤُهُمْ عَنْ الضُّعَفاء الَّذِينَ أضَلُّوهُمْ مَخافَة التَّعْيِير". al-Muyassar 10:54, bare fact only, no audience named: "وأخفى الذين ظلموا حسرتهم حين أبصروا عذاب الله واقعًا بهم جميعًا". Ibn Kathir (English) likewise general: "they would feel in their hearts regret when they see the torment". Attribution is stated per-edition; no 'all four agree' claim is made — the four are explicitly split into two positions. The original interiority reading is preserved but demoted and explicitly marked as contemplation rather than as what the verb means (reviewer's fix (b)), on top of adding the classical gloss (fix (a)).

edits.after:
This is essential. The atmosphere is terrifying, but the ayah anchors it in **qist**. Exact justice. Not rage detached from truth. Not arbitrary crushing. The surah keeps bringing us back to the moral structure of Allah's judgment.

The commentators read *baynahum* — "between them" — in more than one width. Al-Tabari keeps it inside the scene just described: Allah judges that day between the followers and the leaders among them, with fairness. Al-Jalalayn opens it out to all creation. Either way, the verdict is not decided by who managed to hide what.

edits.before: *Qaddat* — Form II of ق د د — to tear, to rip. Intensive form: this was a forceful grab, not a gentle tug. *Qamisahu* — his shirt, from ق م ص. *Min dubur* — from behind, from the back.
edits.after: *Qaddat* — from ق د د — to tear, to split. It is the plain Form I of the verb, so the force in this moment is not coming from the verb's pattern; it is coming from the story. And the story supplies plenty. Ibn Kathir has her catching up with him and holding on to his shirt from the back, "tearing it so terribly that it fell off Yusuf's back," with him still running and her still in pursuit. Al-Tabari has her clinging to the shirt and hauling him back toward her to keep him from reaching the door — and adds the reason the tear landed where it did: because Yusuf was the one fleeing and she was the one pursuing. This was not a gentle tug. *Qamisahu* — his shirt, from ق م ص. *Min dubur* — from behind, from the back.

edits.defect: (b) ADAB/IKHTILAF GAP — a prophet's inner state stated as settled fact, contradicting the file's own lawla-fronted translation, with no tadabbur/'ismah line
edits.before: This matters enormously for how we understand temptation. The passage does not present Yusuf as a superhuman who felt nothing. *Hamma biha* — he inclined toward her. The Quran does not deny this. It presents it honestly: he was human, the conditions were extreme, the desire was real. And then: *lawla an ra'a burhana rabbihi* — "had he not seen the proof of his Lord." The thing that stopped him was not stoicism. It was a gift.
edits.after:
This matters enormously for how we understand temptation. But before going any further, the honest thing is to say plainly that the tradition did not read *wa hamma biha* in one voice, and this reflection is not the place where that gets settled.

One reading takes the sentence in the order it stands: she desired him, he desired her, and what stopped him was the *burhan*. Al-Tabari holds this. He says Allah informed us of the *hamm* of Yusuf and the wife of the 'Aziz, each one of them toward the other, and that the sign Yusuf saw restrained him from going through with what he had inclined toward. Al-Jalalayn is blunter still: he supplies the suppressed answer to *lawla* outright — had he not seen the proof, he would have lain with her.

A second reading fronts the *lawla* — "he would have desired her had he not seen the proof of his Lord" — so that the inclination never actualizes at all. That is the rendering used above in this file, and it is the direction Ibn Kathir leans: he reports from al-Baghawi that the verse "is about the thoughts that cross the mind," and sets beside it the hadith that when a servant intends an evil act and does not do it, and leaves it for Allah's sake, a good deed is written for him instead. Al-Muyassar reads it the same way, and marks the difference between the two people carefully — her self inclined to the act itself, while Yusuf's self spoke to him in passing thoughts. Ibn Kathir also preserves a third report altogether: that the *hamm* meant Yusuf was about to strike her.

None of that is settled here, and none of it should be read as a verdict on *'ismah*, the protection of the prophets. That is a question of *'aqidah*, argued by people trained for it, and a tadabbur is not where it is decided. What can be said without taking a side is the thing every one of these readings shares: whatever the *hamm* was, it was not what saved him. *Lawla an ra'a burhana rabbihi* — "had he not seen the proof of his Lord." The *burhan* came from outside him. The thing that stopped him was not stoicism. It was a gift.

And the sources will not tell us what the gift looked like. Al-Tabari runs through the reports — that Yusuf was shown the form of Ya'qub, or the form of the master of the house, or the warnings Allah revealed about *zina* — and then rules that none of them carries decisive proof over the others, so the right course is to say what Allah said, believe it, and leave the rest to the One who knows. Ibn Kathir quotes him approvingly: it should be left vague, as Allah left it. The passage keeps its own secret.
edits.evidence: Position 1 — al-Tabari 12:24: "وأولى الأقوال في ذلك بالصواب أن يقال: إن الله جل ثناؤه أخبر عن همِّ يوسف وامرأة العزيز كل واحد منهما بصاحبه، لولا أن رأى يوسف برهان ربه، وذلك آيةٌ من الله، زجرته عن ركوب ما همَّ به يوسف من الفاحشة". al-Jalalayn 12:24: "﴿وهَمَّ بِها﴾ قَصَدَ ذَلِكَ ... وجَواب لَوْلا لَجامَعَها". Position 2 — Ibn Kathir 12:24: "This is about the thoughts that cross the mind, according to Al-Baghawi", followed by the Abu Hurayrah hadith "if he intends to commit an evil act but did not commit it, then record it for him as one good deed, if he left it for My sake"; al-Muyassar 12:24: "ولقد مالت نفسها لفعل الفاحشة، وحدَّثت يوسفَ نفسُه حديث خطرات للاستجابة". Third report — Ibn Kathir 12:24: "It was also reported that the Ayah means that Yusuf was about to beat her." Burhan left unspecified — al-Tabari 12:24: "ولا حجة للعذر قاطعة بأيِّ ذلك [كان] من أيٍّ. والصواب أن يقال في ذلك ما قاله الله تبارك وتعالى، والإيمان به، وترك ما عدا ذلك إلى عالمه", quoted by Ibn Kathir as "it should be left vague, as Allah left it." No position is adjudicated; each is attributed to the specific edition that carries it. The self-contradiction is resolved by naming the file's own translation as the second reading rather than silently asserting the first.

edits.defect: (c) EXTRA-TEXTUAL — the wife of the 'Aziz called Yusuf's owner, contradicted by all four editions
edits.before:
Yusuf is a slave in the most powerful household in Egypt. He has no family, no advocate, no legal standing. He is beautiful — the Quran has told us this — and he is alone in a house with the woman who owns him.

She is not named. The Quran calls her *allati huwa fi baytiha* — "she in whose house he is." This is not anonymity. It is a description of **power.** He is in *her* house. He is her property. He eats her food. He sleeps under her roof. The power asymmetry is total.
edits.after:
Yusuf is a slave in the most powerful household in Egypt. He has no family, no advocate, no legal standing. He is beautiful — the Quran has told us this — and he is alone in the house with the wife of the man who bought him.

The ownership is worth getting right, because the verses are precise about it. The buyer and master is the 'Aziz, not his wife. Al-Jalalayn glosses Yusuf's own words *innahu rabbi* as "the one who bought me — my master." Al-Tabari has Yusuf saying it to her face: your companion and your husband is my master. And two verses later the Quran calls the 'Aziz *sayyidaha* — **her** master — standing at the door.

She is not named. The Quran calls her *allati huwa fi baytiha* — "she in whose house he is." That is not anonymity. It is a description of **position.** He is inside her household, under her roof, eating from a table that is not his, with no standing of his own and nobody to speak for him. She is the wife of the man who owns him, and she is the one who will get to tell the story first. The asymmetry does not need exaggerating to be total.
edits.evidence: al-Jalalayn 12:23: "﴿إنّهُ﴾ الَّذِي اشْتَرانِي ﴿رَبِّي﴾ سَيِّدِي ﴿أحْسَنَ مَثْوايَ﴾ مُقامِي فَلا أخُونه فِي أهْله". al-Tabari 12:23: "﴿إنه ربي أحسن مثواي﴾ يقول: إن صاحبك وزوجك سيدي". The Quran's own word at 12:25 is سَيِّدَهَا, glossed by al-Tabari as "وهو زوج المرأة" with chains from Mujahid and (via al-Hasan) Zayd b. Thabit — "السيد الزوج" — and by al-Jalalayn as "﴿سَيِّدها﴾ زَوْجها", al-Muyassar as "ووجدا زوجها عند الباب", Ibn Kathir as "They both found her master (i.e. her husband) at the door." The retained asymmetry (his position in the household, and her control of the first account) is textual: 12:23 allati huwa fi baytiha, 12:25 she speaks first.

edits.defect: (c, cont.) Unverifiable ikhtilaf attribution on innahu rabbi, entangled with the ownership fix
edits.before: **إِنَّهُۥ رَبِّىٓ أَحْسَنَ مَثْوَاىَ** — "He is my lord who has made good my residence." The *hu* (he) here is ambiguous — classical scholars differ on whether it refers to Allah or to the 'Aziz (the master of the house). If it means the 'Aziz: "My master has treated me well — I cannot betray him." If it means Allah: "My Lord has placed me here in good standing — I cannot disobey Him." The ambiguity is load-bearing. Both readings are true simultaneously. Loyalty to the earthly master and loyalty to the divine Master converge in the same refusal. Yusuf doesn't need to choose between gratitude and piety. They demand the same thing.
edits.after:
**إِنَّهُۥ رَبِّىٓ أَحْسَنَ مَثْوَاىَ** — "He is my lord who has made good my residence." The word *rabb* carries both senses in older Arabic: the Lord, and the master of a house. Ibn Kathir notes the usage directly — the chief and master were called *rabb* — and all four commentaries consulted here read the *hu* as the 'Aziz: your husband is my master, he gave me a good place in his house, so I will not betray him with his own wife. Al-Tabari carries it through several chains — al-Suddi, Ibn Abi Najih, Mujahid — and Mujahid spells it out: *sayyidi*, meaning the woman's husband. Al-Muyassar puts the same words in Yusuf's mouth: I take refuge from betraying my master, who made my place here good and treated me generously.

Read that way, the refusal stands on two floors and only one of them is spoken aloud. The first word out of his mouth was *ma'adh Allah*. The next sentence is about a debt owed to a man who treated him well. Loyalty to the earthly master and loyalty to the divine Master land on the same answer, so Yusuf never has to choose between gratitude and piety. They demand the same thing.
edits.evidence: Not on the reviewer's list, but the ownership fix would have contradicted it if left standing, and the claim itself did not verify. NONE of the four fetched editions carries the 'hu = Allah' reading. Ibn Kathir 12:23: "as they used to call the chief and master a 'Rabb', Yusuf said to her, 'your husband is my master who provided me with comfortable living and was kind to me, so I will never betray him by committing immoral sins with his wife,' ... This was said by Mujahid, As-Suddi, Muhammad bin Ishaq and several others." al-Tabari 12:23 asanid 19002 (al-Suddi: سيدي), 19003 (Ibn Abi Najih: سيدي), 19007 (Mujahid: سيدي = يعني: زوج المرأة), 19008 (Ibn Ishaq: يعني إطفير). al-Jalalayn 12:23: "الَّذِي اشْتَرانِي ... سَيِّدِي". al-Muyassar 12:23: "من خيانة سيدي الذي أحسن منزلتي وأكرمني فلا أخونه في أهله". The breadth phrase is scoped to 'all four commentaries consulted here' and each was checked individually — no claim is made about the wider tradition. The file's convergence point (gratitude and piety demand the same refusal) is preserved, now resting on al-Tabari's and al-Muyassar's own framing (ظلم وخيانة لسيدي) rather than on an unverified ambiguity.
